events.title: THE EXPEDITION'S SCRIBES FIX THE GENERAL REGION OF THE NEW COUNTRY
events.body: The field record begins the new week by assigning the country beyond the first difficult pass to a broad central Apennine and Umbrian geographic frame. The scribes compare the terrain, routes, and river directions observed by the expedition with known places used as reference anchors, including Narnia, Interamna Nahars, Spoletium, Fulginium, and Iguvium. The comparison is deliberately written as a regional identification rather than a claim that the column has reached any one of those towns. The expedition's current field record does not fix its temporary camp to a precise settlement. This distinction gives the Roman record a usable geographic context without turning an uncertain position into a false certainty. The new entry is copied into the field book beside the account of the difficult pass crossed during the previous week.

events.title: A LOWER TRACK APPEARS TO LEAD TOWARD THE OLDER UMBRIAN ROAD NETWORK
events.body: A local guide identifies a lower track running away from the difficult ground and toward country that is easier to cross with animals. The track is compared with the expedition's earlier route accounts and with the known Roman road corridor through Umbria. The scribes note that its broader direction can be discussed in relation to the country around Spoletium and Fulginium without recording either place as a destination actually reached. The track itself is not presented as a newly discovered Roman road, only as a route not previously represented in the expedition's own field notes. The party spends part of the day examining its footing and points of water before deciding how much of the route can safely be tested. The investigation consumes part of the expedition's carried provisions and adds another verified route possibility to the record.

events.title: A RELIABLE SPRING CHANGES THE EXPEDITION'S WATER CALCULATION
events.body: While testing the lower track, the expedition finds a dependable hillside spring that is easier to reach than the water source described in the earlier route account. The discovery changes the day's immediate water arrangements and allows the party to refill its carried vessels before continuing. Local inhabitants who know the ground confirm that the spring is used seasonally, although their statements are kept separate from what the expedition has personally observed. The scribes record the location in relation to the surrounding slopes and the route from which it was reached. The finding does not reveal a city or a final destination, but it gives the expedition a safer supply point for the next stage of movement. The water is therefore entered as a verified field observation rather than a rumor.

events.title: THE NEWLY PURCHASED FIELDS REMAIN IN FULL SPRING ROTATION AT THE ESTATE
events.body: At the estate, the newly purchased tract remains in the full rhythm of spring cultivation while the expedition continues beyond the pass. Stewards coordinate watering and field labor with the older acreage and continue to keep the purchased ground separately identified in the property records. Grain and fodder are drawn from the household stores to sustain the longer working days, but no new land is acquired and the tract's ownership remains unchanged. The work maintains the estate's established productive use while placing another ordinary demand on its available provisions. The stewards also preserve the established access arrangements with nearby smallholders so that the new tract does not become the cause of another boundary dispute. The field books therefore record continued cultivation, continued provisioning, and no change to the estate boundary.

events.title: MARCELLUS ASKS FOR THE EXPEDITION'S METHOD OF DISTINGUISHING OBSERVATION FROM TESTIMONY
events.body: A further communication from Marcus Claudius Marcellus reaches the estate concerning the continuing documentary inquiry. Marcellus asks whether the expedition's geographic notes can be kept in the same strict distinction between firsthand observation and later testimony that has been used in the raid dossier associated with Aulus Vettius. The question does not order a route change or impose a destination on the expedition. Valerius's scribes recognize that the same documentary discipline is already being used in the field and prepare the relevant description for preservation with the correspondence. The exchange links the household investigation and the expedition without merging their separate evidence. The Roman archive therefore gains a clearer account of how the expedition is recording uncertain geography without overstating what has been personally observed.

events.title: THE EXPEDITION FINDS A SECONDARY PASSAGE INTO THE UPPER COUNTRY
events.body:
You wake before the camp has fully stirred, with the route papers from the previous days still lying beside the field records.
The difficult pass you crossed has not ended the expedition; it has changed the kind of country you are now trying to understand.
Beyond the camp, the ground appears to divide into several lines of travel, some rising again toward broken slopes and others falling toward lower country.
The purpose of the journey remains the same: continue the newly authorized Roman expedition, examine unfamiliar country directly, and preserve information that can be tested after the party has moved on.
The campaign ledger still records 394 soldiers in the wider establishment, while no separate numerical strength for this expedition detachment has been established in the surviving record.
You therefore make no unsupported count of the men with you, but you pay close attention to how many loads, animals, and route observations the party can actually manage.
The local guide points toward a narrow line between two rising shoulders of ground.
At first it appears to be little more than a rough track used when easier ground becomes difficult.
You walk farther along it yourself before allowing the rest of the party to commit to the passage.
The surface is uneven, but the route is not blocked, and the country ahead falls away more gently than the slope behind the camp.
Then the track bends.
The bend reveals a second passage that was hidden from the camp and from the approach to the first pass.
You stop and look back toward the country already crossed before looking forward again.
What seemed from a distance to be a closed section of high ground is now revealed as a connected system of ridges and lower saddles.
The discovery does not place you inside any named city.
Instead, it gives the scribes something more useful for the commission: a route that can be described and checked against the known geography of central Umbria.
They begin comparing the new passage with the established regional anchors around Narnia, Spoletium, and Fulginium, carefully marking those names as reference points rather than claiming that the expedition has reached them.
The distinction matters because you can now describe the direction and character of the country with greater confidence without pretending to know more than the march has actually shown you.
From the higher ground you can see a sequence of valleys and ridges leading toward country that appears easier to traverse than the immediate slopes around the camp.
The party spends the better part of the day testing the passage instead of merely looking at it from above.
You send the animals through the safer sections first and follow behind them, stopping whenever the footing becomes uncertain.
One of the loads must be steadied as the route narrows, but the column passes without a loss.
The men who have grown used to climbing now have to adjust to a route that alternates between descent and short rises.
You can feel the difference immediately: the pass is no longer one obstacle but part of a broader pattern of movement imposed by the land.
At a sheltered point below the ridge, you stop long enough for the scribes to compare the new route with the earlier accounts.
One account had suggested that the country beyond the first pass would force the expedition back toward the higher ground.
Your direct observation now shows that at least one lower alternative exists.
You do not erase the older account.
Instead, you preserve it beside the new observation, allowing later readers to see exactly where testimony was corrected by field evidence.
By late afternoon the route has become sufficiently clear to enter as a distinct secondary passage in the expedition record.
You choose a temporary stopping place near the route rather than pushing deeper into unfamiliar country after the light begins to fail.
At camp the day's observations are copied while the landscape is still fresh in everyone's memory.
The new passage becomes the most important geographic result of the expedition since the crossing of the first difficult pass.
It gives the journey another viable line of movement and links the immediate country to the broader Apennine landscape without pretending that the destination is known.
You sit with the route sketch and compare its valleys, slopes, and direction against the regional names already entered in the field index.
The names of Narnia, Spoletium, and Fulginium now serve as geographical anchors in the record, not as destinations invented for dramatic effect.
The expedition remains active.
You have not reached Rome, you have not reached a final destination, and you have not returned to any known center.
What you have done is establish a second passage through country that had previously been known to the expedition only through incomplete accounts.
The gain is therefore not a mythical discovery of a forgotten city but a tested route whose usefulness comes from direct observation.
You order the scribes to mark the passage separately from the uncertain testimony collected before the march.
The record now contains two kinds of knowledge: what others said about the country and what your own feet, animals, and route inspections have demonstrated.
The distinction becomes part of the expedition's value.
Before the night is fully dark, you look once more toward the line of country beyond the new passage.
The land remains open in front of you.
The expedition has gained a new route, but it has not yet learned where that route ultimately leads.
For the first time since leaving the previous camp, the uncertainty ahead feels less like a wall and more like a road that can be investigated.

events.title: THE NEW ROUTE REGISTER IS COPIED AND SEALED BEFORE THE NEXT MARCH
events.body: Before the expedition breaks camp again, the scribes prepare a clean copy of the new route register and seal it with the earlier pass account. The copy distinguishes direct observations from guide testimony and preserves the regional place-name anchors separately from the expedition's unresolved exact position. A notation associated with Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer's correspondence is kept with the record because the Roman political connection remains part of the documentary chain surrounding the expedition. The field party therefore begins the next stage with a more precise regional frame and a second tested route, but without a fabricated final destination. The country beyond the new passage remains open for further examination.
